title: TA9-09087
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXXX (the "principal claimant") and his wife, XXXX XXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "female claimant"), who are citizens of Mexico, are making claims for refugee protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1

These claims were joined pursuant to Rule 49(1) of the Refugee Protection Division Rules.2 The Panel is of the opinion that the principal and female claimants must rely on each other's testimony to support their respective claims.
The principal claimant alleged as follows:

The claimant was the XXXX of the of the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX of XXXX XXXX, XXXX, XXXX, Mexico, which was responsible for XXXX XXXX XXXX for the XXXX XXXX. The principal claimant became aware that certain people, who were associated with specific local businesses, were also involved in the illegal trafficking of drugs. The principal claimant informed the police of these fact and his police report came to the attention of these criminals. After filing his report, the principal claimant had at least seven separate encounters with these criminals from XXXX, 2008, until XXXX, 2009 and he sought protection of the police on a number of occasions for the beatings, death threats and attempts made on his life and the female claimant's life; however, he received little or no assistance from the police. Notwithstanding the fact that he and the entire committee resigned from their government positions, the principal and female claimant continued to be threatened and harrassed by this criminal gang.

Fearing that they would eventually be killed by these individuals, the claimants came to Canada on XXXX, 2009, and eventually applied for the protection of the Canadian government as a refugees on XXXX, 2009.
The Panel finds that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor are they persons in need of protection. ANALYSIS Identity
The Panel determines that the claimants' supporting documentation, which includes their genuine Mexican passports3 establishes their identities as a citizens of Mexico. Credibility

The determinative issues in these claims are credibility of the claimants' PIF4 narratives, supporting documentary evidence and their oral testimony, as well as, the issues of state protection and Internal Flight Alternative (IFA).

Credibility is an issue in all claims before the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB). In order to determine whether the claim is well-founded, the Panel must find, on a balance of probabilities, that the evidence is credible and trustworthy. A claimant's testimony is presumed to be true unless there are valid reasons to doubt its truthfulness.5 The existence of contradictions, discrepancies, and implausibilities in the evidence of a claimant is a well-accepted basis for a finding of a lack of credibility. This also applies to omissions in the claimant's previous statements, whether made to Canadian immigration officials at the time of arrival in Canada, in previous examinations under oath or at the hearing of the claim, or in the claimant's PIF. Credibility of the Claimants' Documentary Evidence

A determinative issue that the Panel must consider is the credibility of the claimants' supporting documents with regard to the criminal denunciation6 allegedly filed in Mexico on XXXX, 2008, by the principal claimant. The Panel determines that the claimants have filed a fraudulent document in support of their claims.

The principal claimant was given the opportunity to explain why there was no mention at all in his PIF that he had ever gone to the police on XXXX, 2008, to file a police report. The principal claimant indicated that the individual, XXXX XXXX, who had initially assisted him with his original narrative, which was dated XXXX, 2009, had not included a lot of the information and details that he had supplied to this individual on a computer memory stick to assist in the preparation of his PIF. The Panel notes that question #31 of the PIF states, "On the following two pages, set out in chronological order all the significant events and reasons that have led you to claim refugee protection in Canada. ... Provide details of any steps you took to obtain protection from any authorities in your country and the result." The Panel determines, by relying on common sense, that it is not reasonable that the individual who allegedly assisted the principal claimant would not mention the filing of the Denunciation on XXXX, 2009, since the instructions for question #31 are quite clear with regard to the expectations for the information that is to be contained in the PIF narrative. In addition, the Panel finds that it is not reasonable that the Denunciation was not mentioned in the PIF since the principal claimant was actually in possession of this police document, which was his documentary proof that he was actually attacked by five individuals. Finally, the Panel notes that this information was allegedly supplied to XXXX XXXX on a computer memory stick, which would have been the basis for the outline of the principal claimant's narrative and that the claimant signed the PIF as "complete, true and correct." The Panel relies on case of Bakare, Abeni v. M.E.I.,7 which stands for the proposition that the omission of a significant fact from a claimant's PIF can be the basis for an adverse credibility finding. For all of these reasons, the Panel draws a negative credibility finding with regard to the claimant as a reliable and credible witness since his PIF narrative makes no mention at all of the filing of any police report on XXXX, 2008.
The Panel determines that material aspects of this Denunciation are not credible and that the claimants have proffered a fraudulent document to support their refugee claim.

The principal claimant's PIF8 indicates that five men physically assaulted him at approximately 3:00pm in front of a number of witnesses and he testified that he had personally made this Denunciation on XXXX, 2008. The principal claimant was given the opportunity to explain why this police document was dated XXXX, 2008, if he had allegedly made the report on XXXX, 2008. The principal claimant indicated that he had noticed this error and that he had attempted to have a correction made to the document by the police but the police supervisor had simply informed him that the document could not be corrected since "it was a crime to change the date." Since this error with regard to the date on this Denunciation is so obvious, the Panel is not persuaded that there is no judicial procedure in place to correct deficiencies on police documents. The claimant was also given the opportunity to explain why his PIF time frame of 3:00pm for this incident was not consistent with the Denunciation, which actually stated that this event took place at 6:00pm. The Panel notes that the claimant simply did not explain the discrepancy between 3:00pm and 6:00pm between his PIF narrative and the facts as they are outlined in this Denunciation. In further review, the Panel noted that there were no initials in the margins or a line running through the Denunciation, which is common for copies of official documents issued by the Mexican police. The Panel determines that this document is deficient since it is dated XXXX, 2008, which is six days before the alleged attack took place, the incident time frame of 6:00pm within this document is not consistent with the claimant's PIF narrative of the incident occurring at 3:00pm and the Denunciations has no handwritten markings to attest to the veracity of the Denunciations that the Panel has previously reviewed in other police documents during previous immigration hearings pertaining to Mexico.

In the context of the omission of the principal claimant's filing of a Denunciation with the Mexican police, the wrong filing date on the document, the inconsistency of the time the alleged attack took place and the lack of any handwritten markings attesting to the veracity of this document, the Panel determines that the claimants have proffered a fraudulent document to support their refugee claim. The Panel draws an adverse credibility finding with regard to the principal claimant as a credible and trustworthy witness. Has the Principal Claimant been a Credible and Trustworthy Witness?

The Panel find that the principal claimant lacks credibility and, therefore, it finds that his testimony about being assaulted and threatened by criminals in Mexico not to be credible. The Panel determines that the principal claimant's testimony is not credible due to the lack of independent corroborative documentation, as well as, inconsistent testimony and a number of significant omissions in his PIF narrative with regard to seeking assistance from the police.

During the course of this hearing, the principal claimant was asked to explain a number of significant omissions in his PIF narrative.9 Many of the omissions centered around the fact that the principal claimant made no mention in his PIF narrative that he had gone to the police after the alleged incidents on XXXX, 2008, XXXX, 2008, XXXX 2008, XXXX, 2009, XXXX, 2009, and XXXX, 2009. The principal claimant basically repeated his earlier explanation that the person who had assisted with his PIF narrative had dismissed most of his information as "garbage" that should not be submitted. In the context of the instructions that the principal claimant is to set out what steps he took to get the protection of the local police and the sheer number of times he allegedly went to the police, which the Panel determines is approximately seven occasions during which he allegedly met with police supervisors, the Panel determines it is not reasonable or credible that the person preparing this PIF would make no mention of these events since this individual had this information at his fingertips in the form of a computer memory stick.
The principal claimant was able to supply two medical reports to support his and his wife's refugee claim. The Panel gives little weight to either medical report.

The Panel gives the female claimant's medical report10 little weight since it only refers to her having some problems with regard to her pregnancy on XXXX, 2008, and makes no mention of the cause of these problems, which was allegedly the stress from having being shot at while she and her husband were driving in their vehicle at 11:30pm at night. The second medical report11 mentions the principal claimant being attended to at XXXX (XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX). The Panel assumes this medical report was forwarded to support the principal claimant's oral testimony during the initial sitting of this matter on XXXX, 2010. The Panel determines that this report is inconsistent with the principal claimant's testimony since the principal claimant stated he had gone to a small clinic on XXXX, 2008, and that he had gone to the XXXX medical facility after the alleged XXXX, 2008, incident. The Panel also notes that there is no date on this document attesting as to when it was issued, which makes the document suspect. The Panel also determines that this medical letter does not corroborate the claimant's own testimony with regard to the specific medical facility that he allegedly attended on XXXX, 2008, and, therefore, it gives this supporting document little weight. The Panel finds that the principal claimant's own attempts to corroborate his oral testimony with regard to the XXXX, 2008, alleged assault incident has simply resulted in the principal claimant's earlier testimony being inconsistent. The Panel draws a negative credibility finding with regard to the principal claimant's post-hearing documents not being consistent with regard to the medical facility that he allegedly attended on XXXX, 2008. For these reasons, the Panel draws a negative credibility finding with regard to the claimant as a reliable and trustworthy witness for his inconsistent testimony.

In Maldonado,12 the Federal Court stated, "[i]t has long been held that sworn testimony is to be believed, without corroboration, unless there is good reason not to believe it." According to paragraphs 203 and 204 of the UNHCR Handbook on Procedures and Criteria for Establishing Refugee Status: After the applicant has made a genuine effort to substantiate his story there may still be a lack of evidence for some of his statements. ... it is hardly possible for a refugee to "prove" every part of his case and, indeed, if this were a requirement the majority of refugees would not be recognized. It is therefore frequently necessary to give the applicant the benefit of the doubt. The benefit of the doubt should, however, only be given when all available evidence has been obtained and checked and when the examiner is satisfied as to the applicant's general credibility.13

The Panel determines that there is good reason not to believe the principal claimant's testimony because he has provided no documentary proof at all in the form of any complaints he allegedly made with the prosecutor's office with regard to the specific businesses the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX, XXXX, were having problems with. The principal claimant testified that his mother, a XXXX XXXX XXXX, could not acquire the documents; however, the Panel determines, by using common sense, since the claimant filed these complaints, he was a witness to the alleged businesses not complying with the laws and he was the former XXXX - XXXX of this XXXX XXXX, it is neither reasonable nor credible that the prosecutor's office would not provide him with copies of these documents, since the prosecutor's office would require his testimony in any civil or criminal proceeding that may take place.

Finally, although the principal claimant has provided a number of supporting letters14 from fellow committee members with regard to the alleged events that took place in Mexico, the Panel noted that none of these supporting letters mention any specific events that allegedly took place nor do they identify the Mara Salvatrucha 13 as the criminal organization that was persecuting the claimants. At best, the Panel determines that this supporting correspondence was vague letters of support for the principal claimant while he was the Vice-President of this committee. For these reasons, the Panel gives these supporting letters little weight with regard to any actual description or confirmation of events that allegedly took place in Mexico.

The Panel has previously determined that the principal claimant's was not a credible or witness since his PIF narrative made no mention of the Denunciation he allegedly filed on XXXXX, 2008. As well, the Panel has determined that the Denunciation the principal claimant proffered is a fraudulent document and drew a negative credibility finding with regard to the claimant as a credible and trustworthy witness. Finally, the principal claimant's post-hearing medical report was inconsistent with regard to the hospital he allegedly attended on XXXXX, 2008, and it was undated and, for these reasons, the Panel gave it little evidentiary weight. Finally, the Panel has given little weight to the supporting letters from his fellow municipal employees and the Panel has also noted the lack of independent documentary evidence corroborating key aspects of his claim as well as the sentiment expressed above with regard to paragraphs 203 and 204 of the UNHCR Handbook on Procedures and Criteria for Establishing Refugee Status. For all of the negative and cumulative determinations it has made, the Panel draws a negative inference with respect to the credibility of the principal claimant in general. With regard to the credibility of the evidence that the principal claimant has submitted, the Panel refers to the sentiment expressed in the case of Dan-Ash15 that: ... unless one is prepared to postulate (and accept) unlimited credulity on the part of the Board, there must come a point at which a witness's contradictions will move even the most generous trier of fact to reject his evidence.

The Panel has also considered the case of Sheikh16 which states: ... even without disbelieveing every word [a claimant] has uttered, a...panel may reasonably find him so lacking in credibility that it concludes there is no credible evidence relevant to his claim... In other words, a general finding of a lack of credibility on the part of the [claimant] may conceivably extend to all relevant evidence emanating from his testimony.

In the context of the determinations and negative inferences which are outlined above with regard to the principal claimant's sworn Personal Information Form (PIF)17 narrative and his oral testimony, the Panel's previous determination that the principal claimant has submitted false documentary evidence to the Panel and considering the case law which is noted above, the Panel determines, on a balance of probabilities, that the principal claimant has not provided oral and documentary evidence in support of his refugee claim that is truthful, credible or reliable. Since the Panel determined that the claimants must rely on each other's testimony, the Panel determines that this negative credibility finding extends to the female claimant as well.

Given that the allegations, as outlined in this claim, have been found not to be credible, the Panel need not go on to conduct an analysis of state protection or the issue of an Internal Flight Alternative with regard to the particulars of this claim.

On the basis of the totality of the evidence and the negative findings noted above, the Panel determines that the principal claimant has not satisfied his burden of establishing a serious possibility that he would be persecuted or that he would be personally subjected to a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a risk of torture by any authority in Mexico. Since the Panel noted that the claimants must rely on each other's testimony to support their respective claims, this negative determination by the Panel is fatal to the refugee claims of the principal and female claimant.

The Panel concludes that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division, therefore, rejects their claims. (signed) "Paul G. C.
